entry.sum: An estimator is a rule that turns a sample into a guess $\hat\theta$ for an unknown parameter $\theta$; it is judged by its bias, its variance and their combination, the mean squared error. Maximum likelihood chooses the parameter value under which the observed data were most probable, and for large samples it is consistent, approximately normal, and its variance approaches the Cramér-Rao bound, the smallest possible for an unbiased estimator.
entry.why: Every fitted model, from a polling percentage to the weights of a logistic regression or a neural network trained with cross-entropy loss, is a point estimate, and most of them are maximum likelihood estimates. The bias-variance split explains why the 'obvious' estimator is not always the best one.

links.note: Training a classifier by minimising cross-entropy loss is maximum likelihood estimation, and the bias-variance trade-off governs regularisation and model size.
Fitting a decay constant or a particle mass to counting data is done by maximising a Poisson or Gaussian likelihood, and the Cramér-Rao bound limits the achievable precision of a measurement.
Computing a maximum likelihood estimate is an optimisation problem, usually solved by Newton's method or gradient ascent on the log-likelihood.

refs: Rice, Mathematical Statistics and Data Analysis

blocks.body:
A factory wants the mean lifetime of its bulbs; a pollster wants the fraction of voters who support a measure; a physicist wants the decay rate of an isotope. In each case there is a probability model with an unknown number $\theta$ in it, and a sample $X_1,\dots,X_n$ drawn from that model. Point estimation asks: what single number should we report as our guess for $\theta$, and how do we decide whether one guessing rule is better than another?

This page gives the vocabulary for comparing guesses (bias, variance, mean squared error, consistency), two general recipes for producing them (the method of moments and maximum likelihood), and the main theoretical limit on how good an unbiased guess can be (the Cramér-Rao bound). It relies on [[distributions]] for the models and on [[limit-theorems]] for what happens as $n$ grows.

blocks.title: Estimator
blocks.body:
Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be independent with common density or mass function $f(x;\theta)$, where $\theta$ is unknown. An estimator of $\theta$ is any function $\hat\theta = T(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ of the sample that does not involve $\theta$. Its value on the data actually observed is called the estimate.

The point of the distinction: the estimate is one number, but the estimator is a random variable, because a different sample would give a different value. Its distribution, the sampling distribution, is what we study to judge its quality.

blocks.title: Bias, variance and mean squared error
blocks.body:
Imagine repeating the whole experiment many times and plotting the estimates. Two things can go wrong. The cloud of estimates can be centred in the wrong place, or it can be centred correctly but spread out widely. These are measured by
$$\operatorname{bias}(\hat\theta) = \operatorname{E}[\hat\theta]-\theta, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta) = \operatorname{E}\big[(\hat\theta-\operatorname{E}\hat\theta)^2\big].$$
An estimator with zero bias for every value of $\theta$ is called unbiased. A single number that combines both defects is the mean squared error $\operatorname{MSE}(\hat\theta) = \operatorname{E}[(\hat\theta-\theta)^2]$. Writing $\hat\theta-\theta = (\hat\theta-\operatorname{E}\hat\theta) + (\operatorname{E}\hat\theta-\theta)$, squaring and taking expectations, the cross term vanishes because $\operatorname{E}[\hat\theta-\operatorname{E}\hat\theta]=0$, so
$$\operatorname{MSE}(\hat\theta) = \operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta) + \operatorname{bias}(\hat\theta)^2.$$

The sample mean $\bar X = \frac1n\sum X_i$ is unbiased for the population mean $\mu$, with variance $\sigma^2/n$. For the variance itself the natural guess $\frac1n\sum (X_i-\bar X)^2$ is slightly too small on average; dividing by $n-1$ instead fixes this, as the next theorem shows.

The third property is about large samples. An estimator $\hat\theta_n$ is consistent if $\hat\theta_n \to \theta$ in probability as $n\to\infty$. By the weak law of large numbers $\bar X$ is consistent for $\mu$, and if $g$ is continuous then $g(\bar X)$ is consistent for $g(\mu)$. A sufficient condition for consistency is $\operatorname{MSE}(\hat\theta_n)\to 0$, by Markov's inequality applied to $(\hat\theta_n-\theta)^2$.

blocks.title: The sample variance is unbiased
blocks.body:
If $X_1,\dots,X_n$ ($n\ge 2$) are independent with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$, then
$$S^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i-\bar X)^2 \quad\text{satisfies}\quad \operatorname{E}[S^2] = \sigma^2.$$

Expanding the square, $\sum (X_i-\bar X)^2 = \sum X_i^2 - n\bar X^2$. Now $\operatorname{E}[X_i^2] = \sigma^2+\mu^2$ and $\operatorname{E}[\bar X^2] = \operatorname{Var}(\bar X) + \mu^2 = \sigma^2/n + \mu^2$. Hence
$$\operatorname{E}\Big[\sum (X_i-\bar X)^2\Big] = n(\sigma^2+\mu^2) - n\Big(\frac{\sigma^2}{n}+\mu^2\Big) = (n-1)\sigma^2.$$
Dividing by $n-1$ gives the claim. The intuition: the deviations are measured from $\bar X$, which is fitted to the very same data and so sits closer to them than $\mu$ does; one degree of freedom has been used up.

blocks.title: The method of moments
blocks.body:
The oldest recipe: express the parameter through population moments, then plug in sample moments. If $\operatorname{E}[X] = m(\theta)$, solve $m(\hat\theta) = \bar X$. For example, if $X$ is uniform on $[0,\theta]$ then $\operatorname{E}[X]=\theta/2$, so the moment estimator is $\hat\theta = 2\bar X$. With two parameters one matches the first two moments, and so on.

Moment estimators are easy and, by the law of large numbers, usually consistent. But they can be wasteful or even absurd: on the uniform sample $0.2, 0.3, 1.9$ the mean is $0.8$, so $2\bar X = 1.6$, even though the observation $1.9$ proves $\theta\ge 1.9$.

blocks.title: Likelihood and maximum likelihood estimator
blocks.body:
Given observed data $x_1,\dots,x_n$, the likelihood is the joint density or mass, viewed as a function of the parameter:
$$L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i;\theta), \qquad \ell(\theta) = \log L(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \log f(x_i;\theta).$$
A maximum likelihood estimate (MLE) is a value $\hat\theta$ that maximises $L$, equivalently $\ell$. In smooth cases one solves the likelihood equation $\ell'(\theta) = 0$ and checks that it is a maximum.

In words: among all candidate parameter values, pick the one that makes what you actually saw least surprising. The logarithm turns products into sums and does not move the maximiser.

blocks.title: Three standard calculations
blocks.body:
Bernoulli. If $k$ of $n$ trials succeed, $\ell(p) = k\log p + (n-k)\log(1-p)$, and $\ell'(p) = k/p - (n-k)/(1-p) = 0$ gives $\hat p = k/n$. With $7$ successes in $20$ trials, $\hat p = 0.35$: the MLE is the observed proportion, as common sense demands.

Normal with both parameters unknown. Up to a constant, $\ell(\mu,\sigma^2) = -\frac n2\log\sigma^2 - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum(x_i-\mu)^2$. Setting both partial derivatives to zero gives $\hat\mu = \bar x$ and $\hat\sigma^2 = \frac1n\sum (x_i-\bar x)^2$. Note the divisor $n$: the MLE of $\sigma^2$ is biased, with expectation $\frac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2$. Maximum likelihood does not promise unbiasedness, and the bias here disappears as $n\to\infty$.

Invariance. If $\hat\theta$ is the MLE of $\theta$, then $g(\hat\theta)$ is the MLE of $g(\theta)$ for any function $g$ (for a one-to-one $g$ this is immediate, since re-labelling the parameter does not change where the likelihood peaks). So the MLE of $\sigma$ is $\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2}$, with no extra work.

blocks.title: How good can an unbiased estimator be?
blocks.body:
The score is the derivative of the log-density, $s(X;\theta) = \frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\log f(X;\theta)$. Under regularity conditions (the support of $f$ does not depend on $\theta$, and differentiation under the integral sign is allowed) the score has mean $0$, because $\operatorname{E}[s] = \int \partial_\theta f\,dx = \partial_\theta \int f\,dx = \partial_\theta 1 = 0$. Its variance
$$I(\theta) = \operatorname{E}\big[s(X;\theta)^2\big] = -\operatorname{E}\Big[\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}\log f(X;\theta)\Big]$$
is the Fisher information of one observation. Large $I$ means the log-likelihood is sharply curved at the truth, so the data pin $\theta$ down well. For a Bernoulli$(p)$ variable $I(p) = 1/(p(1-p))$; for a Poisson$(\lambda)$ variable $I(\lambda) = 1/\lambda$. A sample of $n$ independent observations carries information $nI(\theta)$.

blocks.title: Cramér-Rao inequality
blocks.body:
Under the regularity conditions above, if $T = T(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ is an unbiased estimator of $\theta$ with finite variance, then
$$\operatorname{Var}(T) \ge \frac{1}{n\,I(\theta)}.$$

blocks.title: Proof of the Cramér-Rao inequality
blocks.body:
Let $S_n = \sum_{i=1}^n s(X_i;\theta)$ be the score of the whole sample, the derivative of $\log\prod f(X_i;\theta)$. Its terms are independent with mean $0$ and variance $I(\theta)$, so $\operatorname{E}[S_n]=0$ and $\operatorname{Var}(S_n) = nI(\theta)$.

Write $f_n(\mathbf x;\theta)=\prod f(x_i;\theta)$. Unbiasedness says $\int T(\mathbf x) f_n(\mathbf x;\theta)\,d\mathbf x = \theta$ for every $\theta$. Differentiating in $\theta$ (allowed by the regularity assumption) and using $\partial_\theta f_n = f_n\,\partial_\theta\log f_n$,
$$1 = \int T(\mathbf x)\,\partial_\theta \log f_n(\mathbf x;\theta)\, f_n(\mathbf x;\theta)\,d\mathbf x = \operatorname{E}[T S_n] = \operatorname{Cov}(T,S_n),$$
the last step because $\operatorname{E}[S_n]=0$. By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for covariances, $\operatorname{Cov}(T,S_n)^2 \le \operatorname{Var}(T)\operatorname{Var}(S_n)$, that is $1 \le \operatorname{Var}(T)\cdot nI(\theta)$, which rearranges to the bound.

blocks.title: Large-sample behaviour of the MLE
blocks.body:
For a Poisson sample the MLE is $\hat\lambda = \bar X$, with variance $\lambda/n = 1/(nI(\lambda))$: it attains the bound exactly. That is not a coincidence. Under regularity conditions the MLE is consistent and
$$\sqrt{n}\,(\hat\theta_n - \theta) \xrightarrow{d} N\Big(0, \frac{1}{I(\theta)}\Big).$$
Proof sketch: expand the likelihood equation around the truth, $0 = \ell'(\hat\theta) \approx \ell'(\theta) + (\hat\theta-\theta)\ell''(\theta)$. Here $\ell'(\theta)/\sqrt n$ is a normalised sum of independent mean-zero scores, so by the central limit theorem it is approximately $N(0,I(\theta))$, while $-\ell''(\theta)/n \to I(\theta)$ by the law of large numbers. Dividing gives the result. So in large samples the MLE is approximately unbiased and reaches the Cramér-Rao variance; this is why it is the default method, and why $\hat\theta \pm 1.96/\sqrt{nI(\hat\theta)}$ is a standard approximate 95% interval (see [[confidence-intervals]]).

blocks.title: An exponential lifetime
blocks.body: A made-up sample of 5 bulb lifetimes (in thousands of hours) is $2.1,\ 0.7,\ 1.5,\ 3.2,\ 0.5$. Model them as exponential with rate $\lambda$, density $\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$ for $x>0$. Find the MLE of $\lambda$, of the mean lifetime, and of the probability that a bulb lasts more than 2 thousand hours.
blocks.solution:
The log-likelihood is $\ell(\lambda) = n\log\lambda - \lambda\sum x_i$, with $n=5$ and $\sum x_i = 8.0$. Then $\ell'(\lambda) = 5/\lambda - 8 = 0$ gives $\hat\lambda = 5/8 = 0.625$, and $\ell''(\lambda) = -5/\lambda^2 < 0$, so it is a maximum. In general $\hat\lambda = 1/\bar x$.

By invariance, the MLE of the mean $1/\lambda$ is $\bar x = 1.6$, and the MLE of $P(X>2) = e^{-2\lambda}$ is $e^{-1.25} \approx 0.287$.

blocks.title: Uniform on an unknown interval
blocks.body: Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be uniform on $[0,\theta]$. Find the MLE, its bias and its MSE, and compare it with the moment estimator $2\bar X$.
blocks.solution:
The likelihood is $L(\theta) = \theta^{-n}$ if $\theta \ge \max x_i$ and $0$ otherwise. It is decreasing on the allowed range, so it has no stationary point; the maximum is at the boundary, $\hat\theta = M = \max X_i$. (Calculus is not always the way to find an MLE.)

Since $P(M\le y) = (y/\theta)^n$, $M$ has density $ny^{n-1}/\theta^n$ on $[0,\theta]$. Integrating, $\operatorname{E}[M] = \frac{n}{n+1}\theta$, so $M$ underestimates (it can never exceed $\theta$), and
$$\operatorname{MSE}(M) = \frac{2\theta^2}{(n+1)(n+2)}.$$
The rescaled $\frac{n+1}{n}M$ is unbiased with $\operatorname{MSE} = \frac{\theta^2}{n(n+2)}$. The moment estimator is unbiased with $\operatorname{MSE}(2\bar X) = 4\cdot\frac{\theta^2}{12n} = \frac{\theta^2}{3n}$.

For $n=10$ these are about $0.0152\,\theta^2$, $0.0083\,\theta^2$ and $0.0333\,\theta^2$. The estimators built from the maximum have errors of order $1/n^2$, far better than the $1/n$ of $2\bar X$ and even better than the Cramér-Rao rate. There is no contradiction: the support $[0,\theta]$ depends on $\theta$, so the regularity conditions fail.

blocks.title: Serial numbers
blocks.body: Tickets numbered $1,2,\dots,N$ are in a box, with $N$ unknown. We draw $k$ of them without replacement and see largest number $M$. Show that $\hat N = \frac{k+1}{k}M - 1$ is unbiased for $N$, and evaluate it for the draw $14, 37, 52, 61$.
blocks.solution:
For $M = m$ we need the ticket $m$ and $k-1$ tickets from $1,\dots,m-1$, so $P(M=m) = \binom{m-1}{k-1}\big/\binom Nk$ for $k\le m\le N$. Using $m\binom{m-1}{k-1} = k\binom mk$ and the hockey-stick identity $\sum_{m=k}^N \binom mk = \binom{N+1}{k+1}$,
$$\operatorname{E}[M] = \frac{k}{\binom Nk}\sum_{m=k}^{N}\binom mk = \frac{k\binom{N+1}{k+1}}{\binom Nk} = \frac{k(N+1)}{k+1}.$$
Therefore $\operatorname{E}\big[\frac{k+1}{k}M - 1\big] = N+1-1 = N$.

With $k=4$ and $M=61$, $\hat N = \frac54\cdot 61 - 1 = 75.25$. The idea is natural: the $k$ observed numbers split $1,\dots,N$ into $k+1$ gaps of equal expected size, so we add one average gap, roughly $M/k$, above the maximum.

blocks.body:
- Unbiased is not the same as good. An unbiased estimator with huge variance can lose to a slightly biased one with small variance; compare MSE, as in the uniform example.
- Unbiasedness is not preserved by nonlinear maps. $S^2$ is unbiased for $\sigma^2$ but $S$ is biased (low) for $\sigma$, by Jensen's inequality.
- The MLE need not solve $\ell'(\theta)=0$: it can sit on a boundary (uniform), fail to exist, or be one of several local maxima. Always check the shape of the likelihood.
- The likelihood $L(\theta)$ is not a probability distribution for $\theta$; it need not integrate to 1, and a value twice as likely is not twice as probable.
- The Cramér-Rao bound applies only to unbiased estimators under regularity conditions; it is not a universal speed limit.

An estimate without an error bar is incomplete; [[confidence-intervals]] turn the sampling distribution of an estimator into a range of plausible values, and [[hypothesis-testing]] uses likelihoods to compare parameter values (the likelihood-ratio test). The least-squares line of [[linear-regression]] is the MLE when the errors are normal. Bayesian estimation instead combines the likelihood with a prior distribution on $\theta$. Computing an MLE numerically is an optimisation problem, often solved with [[root-finding|Newton's method]] or [[gradient-descent]] on $\ell$, and the expected negative log-likelihood is closely related to [[entropy|cross-entropy]].

1. For a Poisson$(\lambda)$ sample, find the MLE of $\lambda$ and the MLE of $P(X=0)$.
2. Show that for a normal sample the MLE $\hat\sigma^2$ has smaller MSE than $S^2$. (Use $\operatorname{Var}(S^2) = 2\sigma^4/(n-1)$.)
3. For a geometric sample with $P(X=x) = (1-p)^{x-1}p$, $x=1,2,\dots$, find the MLE of $p$ and the Fisher information $I(p)$.
4. In the serial-number problem, what is the smallest value $\hat N$ can take, and when does it happen?

entry.sum: A statistic such as a sample proportion $\hat p$ or a sample mean $\bar x$ changes from sample to sample; its sampling distribution describes that variation, and its standard deviation shrinks like $1/\sqrt n$. A confidence interval reports an estimate together with a margin of error, built so that the method captures the true parameter in a stated fraction (say 95%) of repeated samples.
key: \hat p \pm z^*\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}} \qquad\text{(approximate confidence interval for a proportion)}
entry.why: Every opinion poll's 'plus or minus 3 points', every clinical trial's reported effect size and every error bar on a scientific graph is a confidence interval. Knowing that the margin of error scales like $1/\sqrt n$ tells you that halving it costs four times as much data.

links.note: Experimental results are reported as a value plus or minus an uncertainty, which is a confidence interval built from the standard error of repeated measurements.
Benchmarking and A/B testing report running times or click-through rates with confidence intervals, and Monte Carlo simulations use the same standard-error formula to decide how many samples to draw.

blocks.body:
A poll of 400 voters finds that 58% support a new park. Nobody believes the true figure for the whole town is exactly 58%: a different 400 voters would have given a slightly different answer. The useful question is how far off the 58% might plausibly be. A confidence interval answers it with a range such as "between 53% and 63%", together with a precise statement of how much trust the method deserves.

To build one we need to know how a sample statistic behaves when the sampling is repeated. That behaviour, the sampling distribution, rests on random sampling ([[sampling-design]]), which makes the variation predictable, and on the central limit theorem ([[limit-theorems]]), which gives its shape.

blocks.title: A statistic is a random quantity
blocks.body:
A parameter is a number describing the whole population, such as the true proportion $p$ of supporters. A statistic is a number computed from a random sample of size $n$, such as the sample proportion $\hat p$ (read "p-hat"). If we could repeat the sampling many times, $\hat p$ would take many values. The distribution of those values is the sampling distribution of $\hat p$.

A tiny example makes this concrete. Suppose $p = 0.4$ and we sample $n = 5$ people independently. The number of supporters $K$ is binomial, and $\hat p = K/5$ has this distribution:

- $\hat p = 0$: probability $0.07776$
- $\hat p = 0.2$: probability $0.2592$
- $\hat p = 0.4$: probability $0.3456$
- $\hat p = 0.6$: probability $0.2304$
- $\hat p = 0.8$: probability $0.0768$
- $\hat p = 1$: probability $0.01024$

The values are centred at $0.4$, the true $p$, but the spread is large: with only 5 people, a sample showing $0.8$ or more happens almost 9% of the time. With larger $n$ the same picture becomes narrower and more bell-shaped.

blocks.title: Mean and spread of the sample proportion and the sample mean
blocks.body:
Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be independent, each with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$, and let $\bar X = \frac1n(X_1+\dots+X_n)$. Then
$$\operatorname{E}[\bar X] = \mu, \qquad \operatorname{SD}(\bar X) = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}.$$
In particular, if each $X_i$ is $1$ (success) with probability $p$ and $0$ otherwise, then $\bar X = \hat p$ and
$$\operatorname{E}[\hat p] = p, \qquad \operatorname{SD}(\hat p) = \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}.$$

Expectation is linear, so $\operatorname{E}[\bar X] = \frac1n(\mu+\dots+\mu) = \mu$. Variances of independent variables add, and $\operatorname{Var}(cY) = c^2\operatorname{Var}(Y)$, so
$$\operatorname{Var}(\bar X) = \frac{1}{n^2}\big(\operatorname{Var}(X_1)+\dots+\operatorname{Var}(X_n)\big) = \frac{n\sigma^2}{n^2} = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}.$$
Taking square roots gives $\sigma/\sqrt n$. For a $0/1$ variable, $\operatorname{E}[X_i] = p$ and $\operatorname{E}[X_i^2] = p$, so $\operatorname{Var}(X_i) = p - p^2 = p(1-p)$; substitute this for $\sigma^2$.

blocks.title: Shape: the central limit theorem
blocks.body:
The theorem gives the centre and spread; the central limit theorem gives the shape. For large $n$ the sampling distribution of $\bar X$ is approximately normal, whatever the shape of the population, so
$$Z = \frac{\bar X - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}$$
is approximately standard normal. For a proportion the usual rule of thumb is that the approximation is reasonable when $np \ge 10$ and $n(1-p) \ge 10$ (some textbooks use 5). If the population itself is normal, $\bar X$ is exactly normal for every $n$.

The standard deviation of a statistic has its own name, the standard error, especially when unknown parameters in it are replaced by estimates. For a proportion the standard error is $\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}$.

These formulas assume independent observations. When sampling without replacement from a finite population, the observations are nearly independent if the sample is at most about 10% of the population. The $\sqrt n$ is the key feature: to halve the standard error you need four times as many observations.

blocks.title: From sampling distribution to interval
blocks.body:
For a standard normal $Z$, $P(-1.96 \le Z \le 1.96) \approx 0.95$. Applying this to the standardised $\bar X$,
$$P\Big(-1.96 \le \frac{\bar X-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n} \le 1.96\Big) \approx 0.95.$$
Rearranging the inequalities to isolate $\mu$ gives
$$P\Big(\bar X - 1.96\tfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n} \le \mu \le \bar X + 1.96\tfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\Big) \approx 0.95.$$
The endpoints are random (they depend on the sample) and $\mu$ is fixed. So the random interval $\bar X \pm 1.96\,\sigma/\sqrt n$ contains $\mu$ with probability about $0.95$.

Other confidence levels use other critical values $z^*$, where $P(-z^* \le Z \le z^*)$ equals the level: $z^* \approx 1.645$ for 90%, $1.960$ for 95% and $2.576$ for 99%. Higher confidence means a wider interval. The quantity $z^*\cdot\text{SE}$ is the margin of error.

blocks.title: Confidence interval
blocks.body:
A level $C$ confidence interval for a parameter $\theta$ is a pair of statistics $L \le U$, computed from the sample, such that
$$P(L \le \theta \le U) = C$$
for every possible value of $\theta$ (exactly, or approximately for large samples). The standard large-sample intervals are
$$\hat p \pm z^*\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}} \quad\text{for a proportion}, \qquad \bar x \pm z^*\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n} \quad\text{for a mean with known } \sigma.$$

The probability describes the method, before the data are seen, not a particular interval after the data are seen.

blocks.title: What 95% confidence does and does not mean
blocks.body:
Once the poll gives $(0.532, 0.628)$, the true $p$ is either inside it or not; there is nothing random left. The correct reading is: "this interval was produced by a method that captures the true value in 95% of samples." If 100 pollsters each took their own random sample, about 95 of their intervals would contain $p$, and no pollster could tell from her own data whether hers is one of the misses.

The statement "there is a 95% probability that $p$ lies in $(0.532, 0.628)$" treats $p$ as random. That is the language of Bayesian statistics, which requires a prior distribution for $p$, and it is not what a confidence interval asserts.

Also notice what the margin of error leaves out. It accounts only for random sampling variation. A badly worded question, a sample of volunteers or people refusing to answer can bias the result far more than the margin of error suggests; see [[sampling-design]].

blocks.title: A poll
blocks.body: In a made-up poll, 232 of 400 randomly chosen voters support the park. Give a 95% confidence interval for the proportion of all voters who support it, and check the conditions.
blocks.solution:
Here $\hat p = 232/400 = 0.58$. The successes and failures, 232 and 168, are both at least 10, and 400 is a small fraction of a town's voters, so the normal approximation is reasonable. The standard error is
$$\text{SE} = \sqrt{\frac{0.58 \times 0.42}{400}} \approx 0.02468,$$
so the margin of error is $1.96 \times 0.02468 \approx 0.0484$ and the interval is
$$0.58 \pm 0.048 = (0.532,\ 0.628).$$
We are 95% confident that between about 53% and 63% of voters support the park. Since the whole interval lies above 50%, the data are evidence of majority support, an idea made precise in [[hypothesis-testing]].

blocks.title: A mean with known standard deviation
blocks.body:
Heights of adult women in a region are known to be normally distributed with standard deviation $6$ cm. A made-up random sample of 8 heights (cm) is
$$162,\ 170,\ 158,\ 175,\ 168,\ 166,\ 171,\ 160.$$
Find a 95% confidence interval for the mean height.
blocks.solution:
The sum is $1330$, so $\bar x = 166.25$. Because the population is normal, $\bar X$ is exactly normal even though $n = 8$ is small, and the interval is
$$166.25 \pm 1.96\cdot\frac{6}{\sqrt 8} = 166.25 \pm 4.16 = (162.09,\ 170.41).$$
In practice $\sigma$ is rarely known. If we estimate it by the sample standard deviation, the critical value $1.96$ must be replaced by a larger one from the $t$-distribution; see [[t-tests]].

blocks.title: How large a sample?
blocks.body: A newspaper wants a 95% margin of error of at most 3 percentage points for a proportion, without any idea what the proportion is. How many people must it sample?
blocks.solution:
We need $1.96\sqrt{p(1-p)/n} \le 0.03$. The product $p(1-p)$ is largest at $p = 1/2$, where it equals $1/4$, because $p(1-p) = \tfrac14 - (p-\tfrac12)^2$. So it is enough that
$$1.96\cdot\frac{1}{2\sqrt n} \le 0.03 \iff n \ge \Big(\frac{1.96}{0.06}\Big)^2 \approx 1067.1.$$
A sample of $1068$ guarantees the target whatever $p$ is. This is why so many national polls have about a thousand respondents, whatever the size of the country: the margin depends on $n$, not on the population size.

blocks.title: Comparing two groups
blocks.body: In a made-up experiment, 45 of 150 people shown advert A and 30 of 150 shown advert B bought the product. Give a 95% confidence interval for the difference $p_A - p_B$ of the purchase rates.
blocks.solution:
Conditions: the people were randomly assigned to two separate groups, and each group has at least 10 buyers and 10 non-buyers (45 and 105, 30 and 120). The two groups are independent, so the variance of $\hat p_A - \hat p_B$ is the sum of the two variances, and
$$\text{SE} = \sqrt{\frac{0.30\times 0.70}{150} + \frac{0.20\times 0.80}{150}} \approx 0.0497.$$
The interval is $0.10 \pm 1.96\times 0.0497 = 0.10 \pm 0.097 = (0.003,\ 0.197)$. It lies just above zero, so the data favour advert A, but the size of the advantage is very uncertain: anything from almost nothing to about 20 points is plausible.

blocks.title: When nothing happens: the rule of three
blocks.body: A new process produces $n$ items and none is faulty. The interval $\hat p \pm 1.96\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}$ collapses to the single point $0$, which is clearly too optimistic. Instead, take as plausible all values of $p$ under which seeing no faults has probability at least $0.05$. Show that this set is $[0, p_0]$ with $p_0 = 1 - 0.05^{1/n}$, and that $p_0 < 3/n$.
blocks.solution:
The probability of no faults is $(1-p)^n$, which decreases as $p$ increases. So $(1-p)^n \ge 0.05$ exactly when $1 - p \ge 0.05^{1/n}$, that is $p \le p_0 = 1 - 0.05^{1/n}$.

Write $0.05^{1/n} = e^{-(\ln 20)/n}$. For every $x > 0$ we have $e^{-x} > 1 - x$ (the curve $e^{-x}$ lies above its tangent line at $0$). With $x = (\ln 20)/n$ this gives
$$p_0 = 1 - e^{-(\ln 20)/n} < \frac{\ln 20}{n} < \frac{3}{n},$$
since $\ln 20 \approx 2.996$. For $n = 100$, $p_0 \approx 0.0295$. So after 100 fault-free items we can still only say the fault rate is probably below about 3%. This kind of interval, obtained by collecting the parameter values the data do not reject, is the bridge to [[hypothesis-testing]].

blocks.title: Going further: exact coverage and better intervals
blocks.body:
The proportion interval $\hat p \pm z^*\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}$ is called the Wald interval. Its true coverage can be computed exactly by adding binomial probabilities over all outcomes $k$ whose interval contains $p$. For $n = 400$ and $p = 0.58$ the coverage is about $0.946$, close to the nominal $0.95$. For $n = 20$ and $p = 0.1$ it is only about $0.876$: when $np$ is small the normal approximation fails; for instance $\hat p = 0$, which happens with probability $0.9^{20} \approx 0.12$, gives an interval of zero width.

A better method inverts the approximate test directly: keep every $p$ with $|\hat p - p| \le z^*\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$, using the true $p$ in the standard error rather than $\hat p$. Solving this quadratic inequality in $p$ gives the Wilson interval, which never collapses to a point and has coverage much closer to the nominal level (see Agresti and Coull). For the poll it gives $(0.531, 0.627)$, almost the same as before; the two differ a lot only when $n$ is small or $\hat p$ is near $0$ or $1$.

The general recipe is a pivot: a function of data and parameter, like $(\bar X-\mu)/(\sigma/\sqrt n)$, whose distribution does not depend on the parameter; inverting probability statements about it yields intervals. Intervals and tests are two views of one object: a 95% interval consists of exactly the parameter values that a 5%-level test would not reject. For a systematic theory of the estimators themselves, see [[point-estimation]].

- A 95% interval does not contain 95% of the data, and it does not say that a new observation will fall inside it. It is about the parameter.
- The normal approximation for proportions needs enough successes and failures; with few of either, use an exact or Wilson interval.
- For a difference of two independent groups, the standard errors do not add; their squares (the variances) do.

Confidence intervals and [[hypothesis-testing]] are built from the same sampling distributions. When $\sigma$ must be estimated, the normal critical values give way to the $t$-distribution of [[t-tests]]. The estimators placed at the centre of an interval, and the reason $\hat p$ and $\bar x$ are good choices, are studied in [[point-estimation]]. The same $\sigma/\sqrt n$ error bar controls the accuracy of [[monte-carlo]] simulation.

1. A made-up survey finds that 90 of 250 students walk to school. Compute a 90% confidence interval for the proportion of all students who walk.
2. A 95% interval for a mean is $(48.2, 51.8)$, computed from a sample of 36 with known $\sigma$. What were $\bar x$ and $\sigma$?
3. How large must $n$ be for a 99% margin of error of at most 2 percentage points, with no prior knowledge of $p$?

sources.ref: Agresti & Coull, Approximate is better than 'exact' for interval estimation of binomial proportions, The American Statistician (1998)

entry.sum: A hypothesis test asks whether data are surprising if a default claim, the null hypothesis $H_0$, is true. The p-value is the probability, computed assuming $H_0$, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed; if it is below a chosen significance level $\alpha$ we reject $H_0$, accepting a probability of at most $\alpha$ of rejecting a true null (a Type I error).
key: p\text{-value} = P_{H_0}\big(T \text{ at least as extreme as } t_{\text{obs}}\big)
\alpha = P(\text{reject } H_0 \mid H_0 \text{ true}),\qquad \text{power} = 1-\beta = P(\text{reject } H_0 \mid H_1 \text{ true})
Z = \frac{\bar X-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n} \sim N(0,1) \text{ under } H_0:\ \mu=\mu_0
entry.why: Tests are how medicine decides whether a drug works, how factories detect a machine drifting out of specification and how physicists decide whether a bump in their data is a new particle. Misreading p-values is also one of the main causes of unreproducible published research, so the logic is worth getting exactly right.

links.note: The discovery of a particle is announced when the p-value under the background-only null hypothesis falls below about $3\times 10^{-7}$, the 'five sigma' rule.
A/B tests of website changes are hypothesis tests on two proportions, and the multiple-testing corrections used in large-scale experimentation come from the same theory.
Comparing two models on a benchmark is a hypothesis test, and ignoring the variance across random seeds or test sets leads to claimed improvements that do not reproduce.

blocks.body:
A friend claims his spinner lands on red a quarter of the time. You spin it 20 times and get 9 reds, where you would expect 5. Is the spinner unfair, or was this just chance? Chance can produce almost anything, so the question has to be made sharper: if the friend's claim were true, how unusual would 9 or more reds be?

That is the logic of a hypothesis test. Assume a default claim, work out what data it predicts, and see whether the actual data fit. It uses the sampling distributions of [[confidence-intervals]] and the binomial and normal models of [[distributions]].

blocks.title: The ingredients
blocks.body:
A test has four parts.

1. The null hypothesis $H_0$: the default claim, a precise statement about a parameter, such as $p = 0.25$. It is what we assume while computing probabilities.
2. The alternative hypothesis $H_1$: what we suspect instead. It is one-sided ($p > 0.25$, or $p < 0.25$) or two-sided ($p \ne 0.25$). It must be chosen before looking at the data, from the question being asked.
3. A test statistic $T$: a number computed from the data whose distribution under $H_0$ is known, here the number $X$ of reds, which is binomial $B(20, 0.25)$ if $H_0$ holds.
4. A decision rule, fixed in advance through the significance level $\alpha$, commonly $0.05$.

The test can end in only two ways: reject $H_0$ (the data are evidence for $H_1$), or fail to reject $H_0$ (the data are consistent with $H_0$). Failing to reject is not proof that $H_0$ is true; it may just mean the sample was too small to see a difference.

blocks.title: p-value
blocks.body:
The p-value of an observed statistic $t_{\text{obs}}$ is the probability, computed assuming $H_0$ is true, of obtaining a value of the test statistic at least as extreme as $t_{\text{obs}}$, where "extreme" means in the direction of $H_1$. We reject $H_0$ at level $\alpha$ when the p-value is at most $\alpha$.

A small p-value means the data would be rare if $H_0$ were true. It is not the probability that $H_0$ is true.

blocks.title: The spinner, step by step
blocks.body:
Take $H_0: p = 0.25$ and $H_1: p > 0.25$ at the 5% level. Assuming the spins are independent, each with the same chance of red, under $H_0$ we have $X \sim B(20, 0.25)$, and we observed $X = 9$. Large values favour $H_1$, so
$$\text{p-value} = P(X \ge 9) = \sum_{k=9}^{20}\binom{20}{k}(0.25)^k(0.75)^{20-k} \approx 0.0409.$$
This is below $0.05$, so we reject $H_0$: there is evidence at the 5% level that the spinner lands on red more than a quarter of the time.

An equivalent view uses a critical region, the set of values of $T$ that lead to rejection. Here $P(X\ge 8) \approx 0.102$ and $P(X \ge 9) \approx 0.041$, so the critical region at the 5% level is $X \ge 9$, and the observed $9$ lies in it. Because $X$ is discrete, the actual probability of rejecting a true $H_0$ is $0.041$, a little below the nominal 5%.

For a two-sided alternative $p \ne 0.25$ we would put about $\alpha/2$ in each tail, or double the smaller one-tailed probability to get the p-value.

blocks.title: Two kinds of error
blocks.body:
The decision can go wrong in two ways.

- Type I error: rejecting $H_0$ when it is true. Its probability is the size of the test, at most $\alpha$.
- Type II error: failing to reject $H_0$ when it is false. Its probability is called $\beta$, and it depends on the true value of the parameter.

The power of the test is $1-\beta$, the probability of correctly rejecting a false $H_0$. For the spinner test with critical region $X \ge 9$, if the true probability of red is $p = 0.4$, then $X \sim B(20, 0.4)$ and the power is $P(X\ge 9) \approx 0.404$. Even a fairly strong bias is missed more often than not with only 20 spins.

The two errors pull against each other: shrinking the critical region lowers $\alpha$ but raises $\beta$. The only way to reduce both is more data. Choosing $\alpha$ is a judgement about which mistake is costlier, which is why a courtroom (where $H_0$ is "innocent") demands strong evidence.

blocks.title: Tests based on the normal distribution
blocks.body:
When the test statistic is approximately normal, the p-value comes from the standard normal table. For a mean, with known $\sigma$ and $H_0: \mu = \mu_0$,
$$Z = \frac{\bar X - \mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}$$
is exactly $N(0,1)$ under $H_0$ if the population is normal, and approximately so for large $n$ by the central limit theorem. For a proportion with $H_0: p = p_0$ we use
$$Z = \frac{\hat p - p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}},$$
with the null value $p_0$ in the standard error, because the probabilities are computed assuming $H_0$. Assumptions in both cases: a random sample, independent observations, and a large enough sample for the normal approximation ($np_0$ and $n(1-p_0)$ at least about 10).

At the 5% level the two-sided critical values are $\pm 1.96$, and the one-sided critical value is $1.645$.

There is a direct link with confidence intervals: a two-sided test at level $\alpha$ rejects $\mu = \mu_0$ exactly when $\mu_0$ lies outside the level $1-\alpha$ interval $\bar x \pm z^*\sigma/\sqrt n$, because both statements say $|\bar x - \mu_0| > z^*\sigma/\sqrt n$.

blocks.title: A filling machine
blocks.body: A machine fills bottles with a nominal 500 ml. The fill volume is normal with standard deviation 4 ml. A made-up random sample of 25 bottles has mean $498.2$ ml. Test at the 5% level whether the machine's mean has drifted from 500 ml, and find the power of this test if the true mean is 498 ml.
blocks.solution:
We test $H_0: \mu = 500$ against $H_1: \mu \ne 500$; drift in either direction matters. The standard error is $4/\sqrt{25} = 0.8$, so
$$z = \frac{498.2 - 500}{0.8} = -2.25.$$
The two-sided p-value is $2P(Z \le -2.25) \approx 0.0244 < 0.05$, so we reject $H_0$: there is evidence the machine has drifted.

The test rejects when $\bar x$ is outside $500 \pm 1.96\times 0.8$, that is below $498.432$ or above $501.568$. If $\mu = 498$, then $\bar X \sim N(498, 0.8^2)$ and
$$\text{power} = P(\bar X < 498.432) + P(\bar X > 501.568) \approx 0.705.$$
A drift of 2 ml is caught about 70% of the time with samples of 25.

blocks.title: Is there a majority?
blocks.body: In a made-up poll 232 of 400 randomly chosen voters support a proposal. Test $H_0: p = 0.5$ against $H_1: p > 0.5$.
blocks.solution:
Under $H_0$ the standard error is $\sqrt{0.5\times 0.5/400} = 0.025$, and $\hat p = 0.58$, so
$$z = \frac{0.58-0.5}{0.025} = 3.2, \qquad \text{p-value} = P(Z \ge 3.2) \approx 0.0007.$$
The conditions hold: the voters are a random sample from a large population, and $np_0 = n(1-p_0) = 200 \ge 10$. This is strong evidence of majority support. It agrees with the 95% confidence interval $(0.532, 0.628)$ found in [[confidence-intervals]], which lies entirely above $0.5$.

blocks.title: Tasting tea
blocks.body: A taster claims she can tell whether milk was poured into a cup before or after the tea. She is given 8 cups, told that exactly 4 had milk first, and asked to pick those 4. Under $H_0$ (she is guessing) all choices are equally likely. Find the p-value if she identifies all 4 correctly, and if she gets exactly 3 right.
blocks.solution:
There are $\binom84 = 70$ equally likely ways to choose 4 cups. Exactly one of them is entirely correct, so if she gets all 4 right the p-value is $1/70 \approx 0.0143$, significant at the 5% level.

To get exactly 3 right she must choose 3 of the 4 milk-first cups and 1 of the other 4, which can be done in $\binom43\binom41 = 16$ ways. The p-value for "at least 3 right" is $(16+1)/70 \approx 0.243$: three out of four is entirely consistent with guessing. Notice that this design could never give a p-value below $0.05$ unless she is perfect; a test with too little data has low power by construction.

blocks.title: Tests without a normal model
blocks.body:
Sometimes we cannot assume a normal population. The sign test needs almost nothing. Suppose 10 people each try two diets, and 8 of them lose more weight on diet A. Under $H_0$ (the diets are equally good, and ties do not occur) each person, independently of the others, is equally likely to favour either diet, so the number favouring A is $B(10, 0.5)$. Then
$$P(X \ge 8) = \frac{\binom{10}{8}+\binom{10}{9}+\binom{10}{10}}{2^{10}} = \frac{56}{1024} \approx 0.0547,$$
and the two-sided p-value is $0.109$. The evidence is suggestive but not significant at the 5% level. Such non-parametric tests trade some power for robustness; refinements such as the Wilcoxon signed-rank test also use the sizes of the differences.

blocks.title: Going further: the best test
blocks.body: Why use $\bar X$ or $X$ as the test statistic rather than something else? For two simple hypotheses, each specifying the distribution completely, there is a definitive answer. Write $f_0$ and $f_1$ for the density or mass function of the data under $H_0$ and $H_1$. A test can be described by a function $\phi(x)\in[0,1]$, the probability of rejecting when the data are $x$; its size is $\operatorname{E}_0[\phi]$ and its power is $\operatorname{E}_1[\phi]$.

blocks.title: Neyman-Pearson lemma
blocks.body: Let $k \ge 0$ and let $\phi^*$ be a test that rejects when $f_1(x) > k f_0(x)$ and does not reject when $f_1(x) < k f_0(x)$, with size $\operatorname{E}_0[\phi^*] = \alpha$. Then every test $\phi$ with size $\operatorname{E}_0[\phi] \le \alpha$ has power $\operatorname{E}_1[\phi] \le \operatorname{E}_1[\phi^*]$.

At each point $x$, the product $(\phi^*(x)-\phi(x))(f_1(x) - k f_0(x))$ is non-negative. Indeed, where $f_1 > kf_0$ we have $\phi^* = 1 \ge \phi$; where $f_1 < kf_0$ we have $\phi^* = 0 \le \phi$; and where $f_1 = kf_0$ the second factor is $0$. Summing or integrating over all $x$,
$$\operatorname{E}_1[\phi^*] - \operatorname{E}_1[\phi] \ge k\big(\operatorname{E}_0[\phi^*] - \operatorname{E}_0[\phi]\big) = k\big(\alpha - \operatorname{E}_0[\phi]\big) \ge 0.$$

blocks.title: What the lemma says in practice
blocks.body: The most powerful test rejects when the likelihood ratio $f_1/f_0$ is large. For a normal sample with known $\sigma$ and $H_1: \mu = \mu_1 > \mu_0$, the ratio is an increasing function of $\bar x$, so "reject when $\bar x$ is large" is the most powerful test, and since it does not depend on which $\mu_1 > \mu_0$ was chosen, it is uniformly most powerful against $\mu > \mu_0$. For composite hypotheses the same idea gives the likelihood-ratio test, which compares maximised likelihoods and connects testing to [[point-estimation]].

- The p-value is not the probability that $H_0$ is true, nor the probability that the result was "due to chance". It is a probability about data, computed assuming $H_0$.
- Statistical significance is not practical importance. With a huge sample, a difference too small to matter becomes significant.
- Not rejecting $H_0$ does not prove it; the test may simply have low power.
- Choosing a one-sided alternative after seeing which way the data point halves the p-value dishonestly.
- Running many tests and reporting the significant ones guarantees false discoveries: with 20 independent true nulls at the 5% level, the chance of at least one rejection is $1 - 0.95^{20} \approx 0.64$.
- Every test has assumptions (random sampling, independence, a model for the statistic). A p-value computed under false assumptions means little.

Tests for means when $\sigma$ is unknown, and for comparing several means at once, are in [[t-tests]]. Tests for counts in categories and for independence in two-way tables are in [[chi-square-tests]]. Every two-sided test corresponds to a confidence interval, as in [[confidence-intervals]]. Sequential testing, where data arrive one at a time, leads to [[martingales]].

entry.sum: When the population standard deviation is unknown and is replaced by the sample standard deviation $s$, the standardised mean $(\bar X-\mu)/(s/\sqrt n)$ follows Student's $t$-distribution with $n-1$ degrees of freedom for normal data, which has heavier tails than the normal. One-sample, paired and two-sample $t$ procedures, and the analysis of variance $F$-test for comparing several group means, are all built on this fact.
key: T = \frac{\bar X-\mu}{S/\sqrt n} \sim t_{n-1} \quad\text{for an i.i.d. } N(\mu,\sigma^2) \text{ sample}
entry.why: Almost every comparison of averages in experimental science, from a drug against a placebo to crop yields under three fertilisers, is a $t$-test or an ANOVA. Using the normal critical value $1.96$ with an estimated standard deviation in a small sample makes intervals too narrow and tests reject too often.

links.note: The proof that the $t$ statistic has a $t$-distribution uses the rotation invariance of the multivariate normal and the independence of $\bar X$ and $S^2$ for normal samples.
The ANOVA decomposition of the total sum of squares into between- and within-group parts is Pythagoras' theorem for an orthogonal projection onto the space of group-constant vectors.
Comparing two training methods across random seeds, or the same benchmark items under two models, is a two-sample or paired $t$-test.

refs: Rice, Mathematical Statistics and Data Analysis

blocks.body:
The z-procedures of [[hypothesis-testing]] and [[confidence-intervals]] use the population standard deviation $\sigma$. In real problems $\sigma$ is unknown and has to be estimated from the same data, by the sample standard deviation $s$. For a large sample this barely matters. For a sample of 8 from a normal population, $s$ falls more than 30% below $\sigma$ about one time in six, and then an interval built with $1.96$ is too narrow and a test rejects too often.

In 1908 W. S. Gosset, writing as "Student", worked out the exact distribution of the standardised mean with $s$ in place of $\sigma$, for normal data. That distribution, the $t$-distribution, is the basis for inference about one mean, two means, and, through its cousin the $F$-distribution, many means at once.

blocks.title: Chi-square, t and F distributions
blocks.body:
Let $Z, Z_1, Z_2, \dots$ be independent standard normal variables.

- The chi-square distribution with $
u$ degrees of freedom, $\chi^2_
u$, is the distribution of $Z_1^2+\dots+Z_
u^2$.
- If $V \sim \chi^2_
u$ is independent of $Z$, then $T = Z/\sqrt{V/
u}$ has the $t$-distribution with $
u$ degrees of freedom, $t_
u$.
- If $U \sim \chi^2_a$ and $V \sim \chi^2_b$ are independent, then $(U/a)/(V/b)$ has the $F$-distribution $F_{a,b}$.

The $t_
u$ density is symmetric about $0$ and bell-shaped, with heavier tails than the normal; as $
u	o\infty$, $V/
u 	o 1$ by the law of large numbers and $t_
u$ approaches $N(0,1)$. Note that $T^2 \sim F_{1,
u}$.

blocks.title: How much heavier are the tails?
blocks.body:
The 97.5th percentile $t^*$ of $t_\nu$, the value used for 95% two-sided intervals, shows the effect:

- $\nu = 1$: $12.71$
- $\nu = 2$: $4.30$
- $\nu = 5$: $2.57$
- $\nu = 10$: $2.23$
- $\nu = 30$: $2.04$
- $\nu = 100$: $1.98$

compared with $1.96$ for the normal. With very few observations, the extra uncertainty in $s$ is large and the interval must widen a lot to keep 95% coverage. By $\nu = 30$ the difference is small.

blocks.title: Student's theorem

blocks.body:
Put $Z_i = (X_i-\mu)/\sigma$, independent standard normals; the vector $\mathbf Z = (Z_1,\dots,Z_n)$ has joint density $(2\pi)^{-n/2}e^{-|\mathbf z|^2/2}$, which depends only on the length $|\mathbf z|$. Choose an orthogonal matrix $Q$ whose first row is $(1,\dots,1)/\sqrt n$ (complete this unit vector to an orthonormal basis). Then $\mathbf Y = Q\mathbf Z$ has the same density, because $Q$ preserves lengths and has $|\det Q| = 1$. So $Y_1,\dots,Y_n$ are again independent standard normals.

Now $Y_1 = \sqrt n\,\bar Z$, and since $Q$ preserves length, $\sum Y_i^2 = \sum Z_i^2$. Hence
$$Y_2^2+\dots+Y_n^2 = \sum Z_i^2 - n\bar Z^2 = \sum (Z_i-\bar Z)^2 = \frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2}.$$
The left side is a sum of $n-1$ independent squared standard normals, so it is $\chi^2_{n-1}$, proving 2. It depends only on $Y_2,\dots,Y_n$, while $\bar X = \mu + \sigma Y_1/\sqrt n$ depends only on $Y_1$, proving 1. Finally
$$T = \frac{\sqrt n(\bar X-\mu)/\sigma}{\sqrt{\frac{(n-1)S^2/\sigma^2}{n-1}}} = \frac{Y_1}{\sqrt{(Y_2^2+\dots+Y_n^2)/(n-1)}},$$
which is the definition of $t_{n-1}$. The unknown $\sigma$ cancels, which is exactly why $T$ is useful.

blocks.title: One-sample and paired procedures
blocks.body:
From the theorem, a level $C$ confidence interval for $\mu$ is
$$\bar x \pm t^*_{n-1}\frac{s}{\sqrt n},$$
and a test of $H_0: \mu = \mu_0$ uses $t = (\bar x-\mu_0)/(s/\sqrt n)$ with p-value from $t_{n-1}$. The quantity $s/\sqrt n$ is the standard error of the mean.

Assumptions: independent observations from a normal population. The procedure is fairly robust: for moderate $n$ it works well for roughly symmetric data without outliers, and for large $n$ the central limit theorem takes over. Strong skewness or outliers in a small sample are the danger.

Paired data, such as the same person measured before and after a treatment, are handled by taking differences $d_i$ and applying the one-sample procedure to them. Pairing removes the variation between individuals, which can be much larger than the effect being studied.

blocks.title: One sample
blocks.body:
A manufacturer claims a battery lasts 10 hours on average. A made-up sample of 8 batteries gives lifetimes (hours)
$$10.2,\ 9.6,\ 11.1,\ 10.8,\ 9.9,\ 10.5,\ 11.4,\ 10.7.$$
Give a 95% confidence interval for the mean lifetime and test $H_0: \mu = 10$ against $\mu \ne 10$, assuming the batteries are a random sample from a roughly normal population.
blocks.solution:
The sum is $84.2$, so $\bar x = 10.525$. The squared deviations sum to $2.555$, so $s^2 = 2.555/7 \approx 0.3650$ and $s \approx 0.6042$. The standard error is $s/\sqrt 8 \approx 0.2136$ and $t^*_7 \approx 2.365$, giving
$$10.525 \pm 2.365\times 0.2136 = (10.02,\ 11.03).$$
The test statistic is $t = 0.525/0.2136 \approx 2.458$ on 7 degrees of freedom, with two-sided p-value $\approx 0.044$. At the 5% level we reject $H_0$; consistently, $10$ lies just outside the interval. Had we wrongly used $1.96$, the interval would have been noticeably narrower, $(10.11, 10.94)$.

blocks.title: Paired versus unpaired
blocks.body:
Six made-up patients have systolic blood pressure measured before and after a month on a drug:
$$\text{before: } 142, 150, 138, 155, 147, 160; \qquad \text{after: } 136, 147, 135, 149, 145, 152.$$
Test whether the drug lowers blood pressure, first correctly as paired data, then (wrongly) as two independent samples.
blocks.solution:
The differences before minus after are $6, 3, 3, 6, 2, 8$, with mean $\bar d = 14/3 \approx 4.667$ and standard deviation $s_d \approx 2.338$. So
$$t = \frac{4.667}{2.338/\sqrt 6} \approx 4.889 \quad\text{on 5 degrees of freedom},$$
with two-sided p-value $\approx 0.0045$ (one-sided $\approx 0.0023$). Strong evidence that pressure drops, assuming the differences are a random sample from a roughly normal population. (Without a control group, this shows that pressure fell, not that the drug caused it.)

Treating the columns as independent samples, the pooled two-sample statistic is only $t \approx 1.07$ on 10 degrees of freedom, p-value $\approx 0.31$. The patients differ from one another by up to 25 points, and that variation swamps the 5-point effect unless pairing removes it. The design of the study decides which analysis is correct, not the analyst's preference.

blocks.title: Two independent samples
blocks.body:
For independent samples of sizes $n_1, n_2$ from normal populations, $\bar X_1-\bar X_2$ has standard deviation $\sqrt{\sigma_1^2/n_1+\sigma_2^2/n_2}$. Two versions are in use.

Welch's test estimates each variance separately:
$$t = \frac{\bar x_1-\bar x_2}{\sqrt{s_1^2/n_1+s_2^2/n_2}}.$$
This is not exactly $t$-distributed, but it is close to $t_\nu$ with $\nu$ given by the Welch-Satterthwaite formula
$$\nu = \frac{(s_1^2/n_1+s_2^2/n_2)^2}{\frac{(s_1^2/n_1)^2}{n_1-1}+\frac{(s_2^2/n_2)^2}{n_2-1}}.$$
(A conservative shortcut is $\nu = \min(n_1,n_2)-1$.)

The pooled test assumes $\sigma_1 = \sigma_2$ and estimates the common variance by $s_p^2 = \frac{(n_1-1)s_1^2+(n_2-1)s_2^2}{n_1+n_2-2}$; then $t = (\bar x_1-\bar x_2)/(s_p\sqrt{1/n_1+1/n_2})$ is exactly $t_{n_1+n_2-2}$ under $H_0$. Welch's version is the safer default, since it does not need equal variances.

blocks.title: Welch's test
blocks.body: Made-up reaction times (in hundredths of a second): group A, $23, 25, 21, 27, 24$; group B, $28, 31, 26, 30, 29, 32, 27$. Test whether the means differ, assuming two independent random samples from roughly normal populations (Welch does not need equal variances).
blocks.solution:
Group A: $\bar x_1 = 24$, $s_1^2 = 20/4 = 5$. Group B: $\bar x_2 = 29$, $s_2^2 = 28/6 \approx 4.667$. The standard error is
$$\sqrt{\frac{5}{5}+\frac{4.667}{7}} = \sqrt{\tfrac53} \approx 1.291,$$
so $t = -5/1.291 \approx -3.873$. The Welch-Satterthwaite formula gives $\nu \approx 8.57$, and the two-sided p-value is about $0.004$. The means clearly differ. (The pooled test gives almost the same answer here, $t \approx -3.90$ on 10 degrees of freedom, because the two sample variances are similar.)

blocks.title: Several groups: analysis of variance
blocks.body:
To compare $k$ group means, running all $\binom k2$ pairwise $t$-tests inflates the chance of a false rejection. One-way analysis of variance tests $H_0: \mu_1 = \dots = \mu_k$ in one step. Let group $j$ have $n_j$ observations $x_{j1},\dots$ with mean $\bar x_j$, and let $\bar x$ be the grand mean of all $N = \sum n_j$ observations. Define
$$\mathrm{SST} = \sum_{j,i}(x_{ji}-\bar x)^2,\quad \mathrm{SSB} = \sum_j n_j(\bar x_j-\bar x)^2,\quad \mathrm{SSW} = \sum_{j,i}(x_{ji}-\bar x_j)^2.$$
Then $\mathrm{SST} = \mathrm{SSB}+\mathrm{SSW}$: write $x_{ji}-\bar x = (x_{ji}-\bar x_j)+(\bar x_j-\bar x)$, square and sum; the cross term is $2\sum_j(\bar x_j-\bar x)\sum_i(x_{ji}-\bar x_j) = 0$, since deviations from a group mean sum to zero.

SSB measures how far apart the group means are; SSW measures the noise inside groups. If the groups are independent normal samples with a common variance $\sigma^2$, then $\mathrm{SSW}/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_{N-k}$, and under $H_0$ also $\mathrm{SSB}/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_{k-1}$, independently. (This extends Student's theorem by the same rotation argument.) Hence
$$F = \frac{\mathrm{SSB}/(k-1)}{\mathrm{SSW}/(N-k)} \sim F_{k-1,N-k},$$
and large values of $F$ are evidence against $H_0$. A significant $F$ says that some means differ, not which ones; follow-up comparisons need a multiple-comparison correction.

blocks.title: Three fertilisers
blocks.body: Made-up yields from three fertilisers, four plots each: A: $4, 6, 5, 7$; B: $8, 9, 7, 8$; C: $5, 6, 7, 6$. Carry out a one-way ANOVA, assuming independent plots with normally distributed yields and a common variance (the sample standard deviations, about $1.29$, $0.82$ and $0.82$, are within a factor of 2 of each other).
blocks.solution:
Group means are $5.5$, $8$, $6$; the grand mean is $6.5$. Then
$$\mathrm{SSB} = 4\big((-1)^2+1.5^2+(-0.5)^2\big) = 14, \qquad \mathrm{SSW} = 5 + 2 + 2 = 9,$$
the within-group sums being $(2.25+0.25+0.25+2.25)$, $(0+1+1+0)$ and $(1+0+1+0)$. The total is $\mathrm{SST} = 23$, as it must be. With $k = 3$ and $N = 12$,
$$F = \frac{14/2}{9/9} = 7 \quad\text{on } (2, 9) \text{ degrees of freedom}.$$
The 5% critical value of $F_{2,9}$ is about $4.26$, and the p-value is about $0.015$, so we reject the hypothesis that all three fertilisers give the same mean yield.

blocks.title: Two groups: ANOVA is a t-test
blocks.body: Show that for $k = 2$ groups the ANOVA statistic equals the square of the pooled two-sample $t$ statistic.
blocks.solution:
With $N = n_1+n_2$, the grand mean is $\bar x = (n_1\bar x_1+n_2\bar x_2)/N$, so $\bar x_1-\bar x = \frac{n_2}{N}(\bar x_1-\bar x_2)$ and $\bar x_2-\bar x = -\frac{n_1}{N}(\bar x_1-\bar x_2)$. Therefore
$$\mathrm{SSB} = \frac{n_1n_2^2+n_2n_1^2}{N^2}(\bar x_1-\bar x_2)^2 = \frac{n_1n_2}{N}(\bar x_1-\bar x_2)^2 = \frac{(\bar x_1-\bar x_2)^2}{1/n_1+1/n_2}.$$
Also $\mathrm{SSW} = (n_1-1)s_1^2+(n_2-1)s_2^2 = (N-2)s_p^2$. So
$$F = \frac{\mathrm{SSB}/1}{\mathrm{SSW}/(N-2)} = \frac{(\bar x_1-\bar x_2)^2}{s_p^2(1/n_1+1/n_2)} = t^2.$$
This matches the fact that $T^2 \sim F_{1,\nu}$ when $T\sim t_\nu$, so the two tests give identical p-values.

blocks.body:
- Using $z^* = 1.96$ with an estimated $s$ in a small sample: intervals are too short and tests too eager.
- Analysing paired data as two independent samples (or the reverse). The structure of the data decides.
- The pooled test and ANOVA assume equal variances. A common rule of thumb is that the largest sample standard deviation should be at most about twice the smallest; otherwise use Welch's test.
- Normality matters most for small samples with outliers or strong skew. Check a plot of the data; consider a non-parametric test such as the sign test from [[hypothesis-testing]].
- A significant ANOVA does not identify which groups differ, and many unplanned pairwise tests inflate the error rate.

The $t$ procedures are the standard tools for regression slopes too: in [[linear-regression]] the slope divided by its standard error has a $t$-distribution with $n-2$ degrees of freedom. ANOVA is the special case of a linear model in which the predictors are group indicators, and its sum-of-squares decomposition is the orthogonal projection of [[least-squares]]. The chi-square distribution introduced here returns in [[chi-square-tests]].

2. Explain why a paired design needs only the standard deviation of the differences, and give a situation where pairing would not help.

4. In a one-way ANOVA with 4 groups of 6 observations, what are the degrees of freedom of the $F$ statistic? If $\mathrm{SSB} = 30$ and $\mathrm{SSW} = 100$, compute $F$.

entry.sum: Chi-square tests compare observed counts $O$ in categories with the counts $E$ expected under a null hypothesis, through Pearson's statistic $X^2 = \sum (O-E)^2/E$. For large expected counts $X^2$ is approximately chi-square distributed, with degrees of freedom equal to the number of cells minus one, minus one more for each estimated parameter; this gives tests of goodness of fit and of independence in two-way tables.
key: \text{independence in an } r\times c \text{ table: } E_{ij} = \frac{R_i\,C_j}{N},\qquad \nu = (r-1)(c-1)
entry.why: Whenever data are counts in categories, such as genotypes, survey answers, defect types or dice outcomes, the chi-square test is the standard first check of whether a model fits or whether two classifications are related. It was one of the first general-purpose significance tests, introduced by Karl Pearson in 1900.

links.note: The large-sample chi-square distribution of Pearson's statistic follows from the multivariate central limit theorem for multinomial counts.
Classical frequency analysis compares the letter counts of a ciphertext with those of the language, and a chi-square statistic is a standard score for how well a candidate key or decryption fits.
Test suites for pseudorandom generators and hash functions apply chi-square tests to bucket counts to check that outputs are spread uniformly.

refs: Agresti, An Introduction to Categorical Data Analysis
Rice, Mathematical Statistics and Data Analysis

blocks.body:
A die is thrown 120 times. Each face should come up about 20 times, but of course the counts wobble: perhaps $25, 17, 15, 23, 24, 16$. Is that wobble normal, or is the die loaded? The binomial tests of [[hypothesis-testing]] handle one proportion at a time. Here we have six counts at once, and we want a single measure of how far the whole table is from what the null hypothesis predicts.

The chi-square statistic is that measure. The same idea answers a second common question: in a two-way table of counts, such as transport to school by school, are the two classifications related, or independent?

blocks.title: Measuring distance between observed and expected
blocks.body:
Suppose there are $k$ categories, $n$ independent observations, and under $H_0$ category $i$ has probability $p_i$. The expected count is $E_i = np_i$, and we observe $O_i$. Simply adding the differences $O_i-E_i$ gives zero, because both sets of counts add up to $n$. Squaring fixes the signs, and dividing by $E_i$ puts the cells on a common scale: a difference of 5 is large if 10 were expected and tiny if 1000 were. Pearson's statistic is
$$X^2 = \sum_{i=1}^k \frac{(O_i-E_i)^2}{E_i}.$$
It is $0$ for a perfect fit and grows as the fit worsens.

Why divide by $E_i$ and not by something else? Each $O_i$ is binomial with mean $E_i$ and variance $np_i(1-p_i)$, which is close to $E_i$ when $p_i$ is small. So each term is roughly a squared standardised count. The counts are tied together by $\sum O_i = n$, which costs exactly one degree of freedom, as the theorem below makes precise.

blocks.title: Chi-square distribution
blocks.body:
If $Z_1,\dots,Z_
u$ are independent standard normal variables, the distribution of $Z_1^2+\dots+Z_
u^2$ is the chi-square distribution with $
u$ degrees of freedom, written $\chi^2_
u$. It takes only non-negative values, has mean $
u$ and variance $2
u$, and is skewed to the right, less so as $
u$ grows.

In a test, large values of $X^2$ mean a poor fit, so the p-value is the upper tail $P(\chi^2_
u \ge X^2_{	ext{obs}})$.

blocks.title: Pearson's theorem
blocks.body:
Let $(O_1,\dots,O_k)$ be multinomial with $n$ trials and cell probabilities $p_1,\dots,p_k$, all positive. Then as $n\to\infty$,
$$X^2 = \sum_{i=1}^k\frac{(O_i-np_i)^2}{np_i} \xrightarrow{d} \chi^2_{k-1}.$$
If the $p_i$ depend on $m$ unknown parameters that are estimated from the same counts by an efficient method (such as maximum likelihood on the grouped counts), the limit is $\chi^2_{k-1-m}$.

blocks.title: Proof for two categories, and the idea in general
blocks.body:
For $k = 2$, write $O_1 = X$, $O_2 = n-X$, $p_1 = p$, $p_2 = 1-p$. Then $O_2 - np_2 = -(X-np)$, so
$$X^2 = (X-np)^2\Big(\frac{1}{np}+\frac{1}{n(1-p)}\Big) = \frac{(X-np)^2}{np(1-p)} = Z^2,\qquad Z = \frac{X-np}{\sqrt{np(1-p)}}.$$
By the central limit theorem (see [[limit-theorems]]), $Z$ is approximately $N(0,1)$, so $X^2$ is approximately $\chi^2_1$. The two-category chi-square test is exactly the two-sided z-test for one proportion.

For general $k$, put $Y_i = (O_i-np_i)/\sqrt{np_i}$, so $X^2 = |\mathbf Y|^2$. The multivariate central limit theorem says $\mathbf Y$ is approximately a normal vector. The constraint $\sum O_i = n$ becomes $\sum_i \sqrt{p_i}\,Y_i = 0$: $\mathbf Y$ is orthogonal to the unit vector $\mathbf u = (\sqrt{p_1},\dots,\sqrt{p_k})$. A calculation of the covariances shows that the limiting covariance matrix is $I - \mathbf u\mathbf u^{\mathsf T}$, the orthogonal projection onto the $(k-1)$-dimensional subspace perpendicular to $\mathbf u$. So in suitable orthonormal coordinates the limit is a vector of $k-1$ independent standard normals and one zero, and its squared length is $\chi^2_{k-1}$. Each estimated parameter removes one more dimension in the same way.

blocks.title: Goodness of fit in practice
blocks.body:
The recipe:

1. State $H_0$ (a model for the cell probabilities) and $H_1$ (the model is wrong).
2. Compute expected counts $E_i = np_i$, estimating any unknown parameters from the data.
3. Merge neighbouring categories until every $E_i$ is at least $5$ (a common rule of thumb; some texts accept a few cells down to $1$ if most are at least $5$).
4. Compute $X^2$ and compare with $\chi^2_\nu$, where $\nu$ = (number of cells after merging) $-\,1\,-$ (number of parameters estimated).

Assumptions: the observations are independent and each falls in exactly one category; the counts are raw frequencies, never percentages or measurements. Converting counts to percentages changes $X^2$ and invalidates the test.

blocks.title: Is the die fair?
blocks.body: In 120 made-up throws the faces 1 to 6 appeared $25, 17, 15, 23, 24, 16$ times. Test at the 5% level whether the die is fair.
blocks.solution:
Under $H_0$ every face has probability $1/6$, so each $E_i = 20$. The throws are independent and every expected count is well above 5, so the chi-square approximation applies. The contributions $(O_i-20)^2/20$ are
$$1.25,\ 0.45,\ 1.25,\ 0.45,\ 0.80,\ 0.80,$$
and $X^2 = 5.0$. There are 6 cells and no estimated parameters, so $\nu = 5$. The 5% critical value of $\chi^2_5$ is about $11.07$, and the p-value is $P(\chi^2_5 \ge 5) \approx 0.42$. The data give no evidence that the die is unfair. Note that $\chi^2_5$ has mean $5$, so $X^2 = 5$ is exactly the size of wobble one expects from a fair die.

blocks.title: Fitting a Poisson model
blocks.body: In 80 made-up football matches the number of goals was $0$ in 18 matches, $1$ in 26, $2$ in 22, $3$ in 10 and $4$ in 4 (no match had more). Test whether a Poisson distribution fits.
blocks.solution:
The parameter must be estimated. The mean number of goals is
$$\hat\lambda = \frac{0\cdot 18+1\cdot 26+2\cdot 22+3\cdot 10+4\cdot 4}{80} = \frac{116}{80} = 1.45.$$
With $P(X=j) = e^{-1.45}1.45^j/j!$, the expected counts for $0, 1, 2, 3$ and "$4$ or more" are about $18.77, 27.21, 19.73, 9.53, 4.76$. The last is below $5$, so merge the last two cells into "$3$ or more": observed $14$, expected $14.30$.

Then
$$X^2 \approx 0.031 + 0.054 + 0.262 + 0.006 \approx 0.353.$$
There are 4 cells and one estimated parameter, so $\nu = 4-1-1 = 2$. The p-value is $P(\chi^2_2 \ge 0.353) \approx 0.84$. The Poisson model fits these data well. (Strictly, $\lambda$ should be estimated from the grouped counts for the theorem to apply exactly; using the ungrouped mean is the usual textbook practice and changes little here.)

blocks.title: Two-way tables: independence and homogeneity
blocks.body:
Now each observation is classified two ways, into one of $r$ rows and one of $c$ columns, giving counts $O_{ij}$ with row totals $R_i$, column totals $C_j$ and grand total $N$. The null hypothesis of independence says $$P(\text{row } i \text{ and column } j) = P(\text{row } i)\,P(\text{column } j)$$. Estimating these by $R_i/N$ and $C_j/N$ gives the expected counts
$$E_{ij} = N\cdot\frac{R_i}{N}\cdot\frac{C_j}{N} = \frac{R_iC_j}{N}.$$
The statistic is $X^2 = \sum_{i,j}(O_{ij}-E_{ij})^2/E_{ij}$, with
$$\nu = (rc-1) - (r-1) - (c-1) = (r-1)(c-1)$$
degrees of freedom: $rc$ cells, minus one for the fixed total, minus the $r-1$ and $c-1$ free row and column probabilities that were estimated. Equivalently, once the margins are fixed, only $(r-1)(c-1)$ cells can be filled in freely.

The same arithmetic tests homogeneity: several separate samples (fixed row totals, such as 80 pupils from each school) with the same distribution across the columns. The design differs, independence being one sample classified two ways, but the computation and the reference distribution are the same.

blocks.title: Transport to school
blocks.body:
A made-up survey of 80 pupils at each of two schools records how they travel:
$$\begin{array}{c|ccc|c} & \text{walk} & \text{bus} & \text{car} & \text{total}\\ \hline \text{School A} & 40 & 25 & 15 & 80\\ \text{School B} & 20 & 30 & 30 & 80\\ \hline \text{total} & 60 & 55 & 45 & 160 \end{array}$$
Test whether the distribution of transport is the same at both schools.
blocks.solution:
Under $H_0$, $E_{ij} = R_iC_j/N$. Both row totals are $80$, so in each row the expected counts are $80\cdot 60/160 = 30$, $80\cdot 55/160 = 27.5$ and $80\cdot 45/160 = 22.5$. Then
$$X^2 = 2\Big(\frac{10^2}{30} + \frac{2.5^2}{27.5} + \frac{7.5^2}{22.5}\Big) = 2\,(3.333+0.227+2.5) \approx 12.12,$$
using that the deviations in row B are the negatives of those in row A. The pupils are independent random samples from the two schools and the smallest expected count is $22.5$, so the approximation is safe. With $\nu = (2-1)(3-1) = 2$, the 5% critical value is about $5.99$ and the p-value is about $0.0023$. Reject $H_0$: travel habits differ between the schools. Looking at the largest contributions shows where: School A has many more walkers and fewer car journeys than expected.

blocks.title: A formula for 2-by-2 tables
blocks.body:
For a $2\times 2$ table with cells $a, b$ (first row) and $c, d$ (second row), $N = a+b+c+d$, show that
$$X^2 = \frac{N(ad-bc)^2}{(a+b)(c+d)(a+c)(b+d)}.$$
blocks.solution:
Write the row totals as $R_1 = a+b$, $R_2 = c+d$ and the column totals as $C_1 = a+c$, $C_2 = b+d$. Then
$$O_{11}-E_{11} = a - \frac{(a+b)(a+c)}{N} = \frac{a(a+b+c+d)-(a+b)(a+c)}{N} = \frac{ad-bc}{N}.$$
Because each row and column of $O-E$ sums to zero, the other three deviations are $\pm(ad-bc)/N$. Hence
$$X^2 = \frac{(ad-bc)^2}{N^2}\Big(\frac{1}{E_{11}}+\frac{1}{E_{12}}+\frac{1}{E_{21}}+\frac{1}{E_{22}}\Big).$$
With $E_{ij} = R_iC_j/N$, the bracket is $\frac{N}{R_1C_1}+\frac{N}{R_1C_2}+\frac{N}{R_2C_1}+\frac{N}{R_2C_2} = \frac{N(R_1+R_2)(C_1+C_2)}{R_1R_2C_1C_2} = \frac{N^3}{R_1R_2C_1C_2}$. Multiplying gives the formula. In particular $X^2 = 0$ exactly when $ad = bc$, that is, when the two rows are proportional.

blocks.title: Going further
blocks.body: Pearson's $X^2$ is one of a family of statistics with the same limit. The likelihood-ratio statistic $G^2 = 2\sum O\ln(O/E)$ is the likelihood-ratio test (see [[hypothesis-testing]]) applied to multinomial counts; expanding $\ln(1+x) \approx x - x^2/2$ shows $G^2 \approx X^2$ when $O$ is close to $E$. When expected counts are small, the approximation fails; for $2\times 2$ tables Fisher's exact test computes the p-value from the hypergeometric distribution of one cell given the margins, as in the tea-tasting example of [[hypothesis-testing]]. A different chi-square test, for a single variance, uses the fact from [[t-tests]] that $(n-1)S^2/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_{n-1}$ for normal data.

- Use counts, never percentages or means.
- Expected counts, not observed ones, must be large enough; merge categories when needed, and recount the cells.
- Subtract one degree of freedom for every parameter estimated from the data.
- The test is one-sided in the upper tail. A suspiciously small $X^2$ (an unbelievably good fit) is not evidence for $H_0$, though it can be a sign that data were adjusted.
- A significant test of independence says the variables are associated, not that one causes the other.
- Each individual must be counted once; the observations must be independent (no repeated measurements on the same person in different cells).

The chi-square distribution is built from the normal one, so it belongs with [[distributions]] and [[t-tests]]. The two-category case is the z-test for a proportion from [[hypothesis-testing]]. The multinomial model behind the theorem appears again in information theory, where $G^2/(2N)$ is the empirical Kullback-Leibler divergence related to [[entropy]].

1. A made-up sample of 200 seeds produced 152 yellow and 48 green plants. Test at the 5% level the genetic model with ratio $3:1$, and check your answer with the z-test for a proportion.
2. A $3\times 4$ contingency table is tested for independence. How many degrees of freedom does $X^2$ have, and why?
3. Show that $X^2 = \sum O_i^2/E_i - n$ for a goodness-of-fit test with $\sum O_i = \sum E_i = n$.
4. Use the $2\times 2$ formula to compute $X^2$ for the table with rows $(30, 10)$ and $(20, 20)$.
